input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "By six on Thursday morning, Mara Venn had opened the blue canvas stall at the east entrance of Bellmarket. The delivery van from North Quay Produce was due before the first commuter rush, and its crates were needed for the day’s display of greens and apples. Rain had stopped during the night, but the paving stones were still slick. Mara put a rubber mat beside the counter and moved the weighing scale away from the edge, where passing shoppers sometimes caught its cord with their bags.

The order sheet listed thirty-two bunches of chard, twenty-four heads of fennel, eighteen kilograms of Cox apples, and twelve jars of orchard honey. Mara had asked for the honey to arrive in its cardboard tray because the jars were easier to count that way. The driver, Ellis, had called at 5:42 to say the van was delayed by roadworks near the canal bridge. He gave an estimated arrival time of 6:20, though he could not say how long the queue would last. Mara used the extra minutes to arrange the chalkboard and set out paper bags.

At 6:27, Ellis backed into the loading bay with the hazard lights blinking. His delivery note showed the produce quantities and a separate line for the returnable crate deposit. Mara checked that line before signing. The deposit was £18, and it was not part of the £146.40 charge for the food and honey. Ellis confirmed that the amount due for the order itself was £146.40; the deposit would be credited when the empty crates were collected. Mara wrote both amounts in the stall ledger so the till record would not combine them.

They unloaded the van in three trips. The chard was packed in shallow green boxes, while the fennel had been secured with paper bands inside a deeper crate. One box of apples had a damp corner, but the fruit inside was firm and unmarked. Ellis set the honey tray on the counter rather than stacking it with the produce. Mara counted the jars twice and found all twelve in place. She then checked the apple weight on the stall scale, which read 18.2 kilograms, two hundred grams above the order. Ellis noted the difference on his copy of the delivery sheet.

Mara’s handwritten receiving notes were arranged as follows:

1. Chard: 32 bunches received; leaves fresh, with two outer leaves removed from one bunch.
2. Fennel: 24 heads received; three had short stems, but all were sound.
3. Apples: 18.2 kilograms received; the additional 0.2 kilograms were not added to the invoice.
4. Honey: 12 jars received in one tray; seals intact.

The last point mattered because the morning total was being checked against a market voucher that covered food purchases but not container deposits. Mara entered £146.40 under produce and pantry goods, then recorded the £18 deposit in the separate returnables column. The voucher balance showed £160, leaving £13.60 available for another eligible purchase. She did not include the deposit when calculating that balance. Ellis initialled the note beside the two amounts, and Mara kept the yellow copy with the week’s other supplier records.

“Can you put the empty crates on the north side when you’re finished?” Ellis asked. “The collection driver comes after lunch, and he needs a clear path to the drain.” Mara pointed out that the flower stall next door sometimes left buckets in that space. Ellis said he would tell the collection driver to wait by the awning if the route was blocked. They agreed that the crates could stay behind Mara’s counter until then, as long as the honey tray was not put on top of them.

A customer arrived while Ellis was securing the van door and asked whether the apples were local. Mara showed him the label, which named the orchard outside Linton but did not give a picking date. She explained that the farm delivered twice a week and that this batch had come in that morning. The customer bought a paper bag of apples and two bunches of chard. Mara weighed the apples separately from the delivery check, charged the displayed stall price, and gave him the small receipt from the till. The sale did not change the figures in the supplier ledger.

Before leaving, Ellis took a photograph of the signed delivery sheet for the depot records. Mara asked him to make sure the image showed the note about the extra apple weight and the separate deposit, because both details were easy to miss on the narrow form. He checked the picture on his phone, then sent it to the depot while standing beside the van. The loading bay was clear again by 6:51, and Mara brought the rubber mat back under the counter.

The rest of the morning brought steady foot traffic but no further delivery. Mara moved the fennel into a wooden crate, placed the honey on the upper shelf, and kept the chard misted beneath a damp cloth. At 12:35, she stacked the empty returnable crates behind the counter with their labels facing outward. The flower stall’s buckets were still beside the drain, so she left the north-side route open and wrote a note for the collection driver directing him to the awning.
